summary: Collects the most critical operational considerations for deploying BGPsec. It expects practices to change as BGPsec is formalized and initially deployed. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A tips-and-warnings sheet for people setting up the signed-route system in real networks.

subtitle: Practical advice for operators rolling out signed BGP paths: keys, partial deployment, routing policy and clocks.

tldr.problem: BGPsec adds cryptographic signatures to BGP paths, but deploying it raises operational questions about keys, partial rollout, policy and time that the protocol itself does not answer.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects the most critical and universal considerations: how to handle RPKI data and router certificates, which routers should speak BGPsec, how edge sites can only sign, how to treat Not Valid paths, and how accurate router clocks must be.
tldr.outcome: It is a best current practice that expects the advice to evolve as BGPsec is formalized and initially deployed.

today: RFC 8207 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 211) published in September 2017. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text itself expects operational practices to evolve as BGPsec is formalized and initially deployed.

sections.title: Why Operations Need Their Own Document
sections.content:
Origin validation based on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is in its early phases. BGPsec (RFC 8205) may require larger memory and more modern CPUs, so it is expected to be deployed incrementally over a longer time span. This RFC describes the operational considerations of that rollout, and warns that they will likely change over time.

BGPsec needs to be spoken only by an Autonomous System's eBGP-speaking border routers. It is designed so that it can protect announcements originated by resource-constrained edge routers. The reader is assumed to know BGP (RFC 4271), BGPsec, the RPKI (RFC 6480), the RPKI repository structure (RFC 6481) and Route Origin Authorizations (RFC 6482).
sections.plainLanguage: Sending signed routes is new, so people running big networks need tips. This document gathers the most important ones.

sections.title: RPKI Data and Router Certificates
sections.content:
For RPKI certificates, CRLs, manifests, Ghostbusters Records, Trust Anchor Locators, cache synchronization and validation, the considerations in the RPKI Distribution and Maintenance section of RFC 7115 apply. Considerations specific to ROA objects do not apply here.

BGPsec-speaking routers can generate their own key pairs and have their certificates signed and published in the RPKI by the RPKI Certification Authority system, or they can be given key pairs by the operator. An operator may use one certificate and key in all routers, one per router, or any granularity in between. A large operator worried that one router's compromise would expose the others may accept a more complex key distribution burden. An edge site with one or two routers may simply use a single key.

Because keys might be compromised, a prudent operator SHOULD pre-provision each router's next key in the RPKI so there is no propagation delay when it is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router needs its own stamp, and a careful operator prepares the next stamp in advance in case the first one is stolen.

sections.title: Deploying Within a Network and at the Edge
sections.content:
BGPsec is spoken by the edge routers that border other ASes. Where edge routers inject BGPsec paths into iBGP, Route Reflectors MUST have BGPsec enabled if and only if there are eBGP speakers in their client cone. The deployment can be incremental, and eBGP speakers facing more critical peers, upstreams or downstreams are candidates for early deployment. Both signing one's own announcements and validating received ones should be considered in partial deployment.

BGPsec, like any policy change, can cause traffic shifts, so a prudent operator has the tools to predict and measure them. BGPsec does not sign over communities, so they are not formally trustable, and an eBGP listener SHOULD NOT strongly trust unsigned security signaling such as communities received across a trust boundary. Outsourcing verification is also not prudent.

An edge site that provides no transit and trusts its upstreams may only originate signed announcements and not validate received ones. Capability negotiation lets a resource-constrained edge router hold only its own signing keys and sign, without receiving signed announcements, so it avoids most of the RPKI. The RFC notes that the vast majority of ASes are stubs and announce the majority of prefixes, which makes incremental deployment simpler and cheaper.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with the doors that face outsiders. Small neighborhoods can just stamp their own letters without checking everyone else's.

sections.title: Routing Policy for Valid and Not Valid Paths
sections.content:
Signed paths cannot cross non-BGPsec topology, so partial deployment forms islands of assured paths that grow and merge. Unlike RPKI origin validation, BGPsec marks a path only as Valid or Not Valid, with no explicit NotFound state. An unsigned BGP4 path is in some sense the equivalent of NotFound. How the result is used is up to local policy.

Should a Not Valid path be discarded? Giving it a very low local preference means it is used only if there is no alternative, but the RFC recommends dropping. Local preference affects only routes to the same set of destinations, so with longest-match forwarding a Not Valid more-specific route can still attract traffic and accepting it is often the equivalent of treating it as fully Valid.

Not Valid paths that are chosen as best path and propagated MUST NOT have signatures stripped, and MUST be signed if sent to external BGPsec speakers, because RPKI propagation timing can make a path invalid at one router and valid at another. Validation state can be conveyed with local mechanisms such as a community, local-preference or MED. A BGPsec speaker SHOULD also perform origin validation per RFC 6811 and RFC 7115.

Route servers must sign per client, including their own AS, but use a pCount of 0 to keep the effective AS hop count and thus their transparency. Routers MUST disallow a pCount of 0 by default, and SHOULD accept it from a neighbor known to be a transparent route server. To protect confederation internals (RFC 5065), a speaker exporting to a non-member removes all intra-confederation Secure_Path Segments.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter fails the stamp check, the safest move is to throw it away. Keeping it at low priority does not really help, because it may still be the best route to some addresses.

sections.title: Replay, Consistency, Contacts and Clocks
sections.content:
To protect against replays of BGP data a day or more old, rekeying routers with keys provisioned earlier in the RPKI is sufficient. A router that once negotiated BGPsec should not be expected to always do so.

Like the DNS, the global RPKI offers only a loosely consistent view, so different caches or routers may hold different data. The RFC says there is no fix for this. Operators who manage certificates SHOULD publish RPKI Ghostbusters Records (RFC 6493) for certificates on which others' routing depends, and should prepare for algorithm transitions (RFC 6916), which will be rare and slow-paced.

Because certificates and ROAs are time dependent, router clocks MUST be correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour, typically by running time servers such as NTP (RFC 5905). A router that believes its clock is seriously wrong, for example a time earlier than 2011, SHOULD NOT validate incoming updates until it is within reasonable tolerance.
sections.plainLanguage: Clocks matter because stamps have dates. A router that thinks it is still the year 2010 should not judge any stamps.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document only describes operational considerations. It states that the security considerations for BGPsec are described in RFC 8205. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This sheet gives tips only. The real safety rules are in the main BGPsec document.

items.title: Not Valid paths
items.text: Recommended to drop; if propagated, never strip signatures.

items.title: pCount of 0
items.text: Disallowed by default; accept only from known transparent route servers.

items.title: Communities
items.text: Unsigned, so do not strongly trust them across a trust boundary.

items.title: Router clocks
items.text: Correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour.

items.title: Next key
items.text: Pre-provision each router's next key in the RPKI.
